strengths: The paper addresses a practical and well-motivated limitation of current REC methods: image-text contrastive learning depends on fine-grained image-text alignment and is constrained by the small number of available negative referring expressions. The proposed shift to image-space contrastive learning is simple, intuitive, and empirically effective.

The method is presented as a general, plug-in framework that replaces the original image-text contrastive objective without architectural changes, making it easy to integrate into existing REC architectures.

The empirical evidence is strong: C-REX consistently improves GroundingREC, CAD-GD, and a GroundingDINO-based baseline on REC-8K across Swin-T and Swin-B backbones and across MAE, RMSE, precision, recall, and F1, establishing state-of-the-art results for REC.

The ablation studies are informative and support the main design choices: image-space CL outperforms image-text CL and their combination, bipartite matching is better than simple top-N selection for positives, and using only positives as anchors improves over the standard supervised contrastive objective.

The paper includes useful supplementary material, qualitative comparisons, failure cases, paraphrase robustness analysis, and comparison to a foundation VLM, which helps characterize the method's scope and limitations.
The writing is clear, the method is easy to follow, and the implementation details are mostly sufficient for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is moderate: supervised contrastive learning in the visual embedding space and bipartite matching are existing techniques. The contribution is largely an adaptation of these ideas to REC with strong empirical validation, rather than a fundamentally new learning algorithm.

There is a potential confound in the central comparison. C-REX uses ground-truth bipartite matching to define positive visual tokens, while the image-text contrastive baselines do not use this matching. The gains may therefore stem partly from stronger localization-based supervision rather than from the embedding space alone; a more controlled comparison, such as image-text CL with matched positives or image-space CL without matched positives, would better isolate the claimed effect.

The class-agnostic counting extension is mixed. On FSC-147, GroundingREC + C-REX actually worsens test MAE from 10.12 to 12.46, despite the abstract/introduction suggesting general improvement. The paper acknowledges this in the body, but some claims remain a bit broad.

Robustness to paraphrased referring expressions is not universal: for CAD-GD, the baseline performs better than the C-REX variant on the paraphrased test set, which weakens the robustness claim even though the paper notes this result.

Some experimental fairness details could be clearer. For GroundingREC, the baseline is taken from a public checkpoint while C-REX variants are retrained, and training schedules/protocols may differ across models. No statistical significance tests or confidence intervals are reported, and several F1/precision/recall gains are modest.

The argument that image-space contrastive learning avoids negative-sample scarcity is plausible but not rigorously analyzed; the paper mainly relies on intuitive arguments and anecdotal evidence, especially for dense scenes where the number of available negative visual tokens may shrink.
The abstract wording overstates the scope of the class-agnostic counting results by implying universal improvement, whereas the evidence shows only mixed and architecture-dependent gains outside REC.

strengths: The paper identifies a clear and practically relevant limitation of prior REC methods: image-text contrastive learning relies on limited negative prompts and suffers from image-text embedding misalignment. The proposed C-REX directly addresses this by moving contrastive supervision entirely into the image embedding space.

The method is simple, general, and well motivated. C-REX replaces the image-text contrastive loss with an image-space supervised contrastive loss over visual tokens, using bipartite matching to define positives, and modifies the supervised contrastive objective to anchor only positive samples so that heterogeneous negatives are not artificially clustered.

The empirical evaluation is extensive and convincing. C-REX is integrated into three different REC architectures (GroundingREC, CAD-GD, and a GroundingDINO baseline) and consistently improves MAE, RMSE, and F1 on REC-8K, often setting new state-of-the-art results.

Ablation studies are informative: they compare image-text vs. image-space vs. combined contrastive learning, evaluate different positive-sample selection strategies, and validate the proposed supervised contrastive modification. These analyses support the central design choices.

The framework shows generality beyond REC by being adapted to class-agnostic counting on FSC-147, and the authors also evaluate robustness to paraphrased referring expressions and compare against a modern VLM (Molmo).
The paper is clearly written, with helpful diagrams and detailed implementation/training settings that improve reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core idea—contrastive learning in the image embedding space—is not entirely new; related works in person re-identification and dense visual representation learning have explored image-space contrastive objectives. The contribution is therefore somewhat incremental, with novelty lying mainly in adapting this idea to REC via bipartite matching and positive-only anchoring.

The comparison against image-text contrastive learning may be partially confounded. C-REX benefits not only from operating in image space but also from bipartite matching to ground-truth points and a much larger pool of negative visual tokens; the paper does not fully isolate how much of the gain comes from the embedding space versus the richer supervision signal.

Some results are mixed. For example, CAD-GD† does not consistently improve (e.g., validation RMSE slightly worsens), and in class-agnostic counting C-REX does not uniformly help all architectures (GroundingREC’s test MAE degrades). The paraphrase robustness experiment also shows the CAD-GD baseline performing better.

There are minor inconsistencies across tables, e.g., GroundingDINO test RMSE appears as 17.93 in Table 1 but 19.73 for the corresponding baseline in Table 4b. Such discrepancies make direct cross-table comparisons less transparent and should be clarified.

The paper argues that image-space CL is the “right” embedding space but provides mostly empirical evidence. A deeper analysis of why image-space supervision avoids the semantic entanglement of image-text CL—and under what conditions image-text CL could approach this performance—would strengthen the conceptual contribution.

Limitations of the method are not discussed in depth, e.g., dependence on accurate bipartite matching, behaviour in extremely dense scenes where few negative visual tokens remain, and the lack of a clear code-release statement.
